boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's action at Steken (Stecken, Stöcken; 5 December 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Archduke Ferdinand's attack on Wrede's Bavarian corps in its positions at Stecken and Wonau, its retreat by Pfauendorf and the Sandhöfe and its evacuation of Iglau in the night. Wrede's attack on Stecken of 3 December (Völderndorff), the outpost fights after 27 November and the truce and evacuation of Iglau after Austerlitz are context. Side A is the Bavarian corps, an ally of France. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Austrian) 17 battalions, 2,000 horse and 40 guns, 11,000 men, under Archduke Ferdinand of Austria, and side A (Bavarian) 10 battalions and 8 squadrons, 7,000 men, under GM Wrede. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 17 battalions, 2,000 horse and 40 guns for side B are Völderndorff's (claim voelderndorff-side-b); his 11,000 is not in the passages read, and the other accounts differ: Völderndorff has the Bavarians hold against an army 30,000 strong, and Schönhals gives the Archduke's corps 13 battalions and about 18 squadrons, 8294 men, by an undated report of the Archduke that he gives after the corps' junction at Czaslau on 24 November (claim schoenhals-side-b). His 10 battalions, 8 squadrons and 7,000 for side A are not in the passages read; neither other account gives side A's strength on 5 December (claims voelderndorff-side-a and schoenhals-side-a). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the Austrians (17 battalions, 2,000 horse, 40 guns = 11,000 men) under Archduke Ferdinand of Austria over the Bavarians (10 battalions, 8 squadrons = 7,000 men) under GM Wrede'.

claims.value: Side A (Bavarian), its own account in Völderndorff: when Bernadotte left with his divisions for Brünn on 29 November, only the Bavarians were left facing the Archduke's corps; Wrede had three regiments of horse but barely 400 serviceable horses among them, and no more than 4,500 foot with six guns, having had to leave as many guns at Mautern by order to cover the army's baggage; Mezanelli's brigade could arrive only in five days, General Karg's in seven and the 4th Chevauxlegers Regiment Bubenhofen after four. On 5 December one battalion of the 7th Line Regiment held the market town of Stecken and the other the heights behind it; to the left stood the first and second battalions of the third Line Regiment (Herzog Karl), the light battalion Dietfurth and the 2nd Chevauxlegers Regiment with a battery; to the right the second and, at Wonnau, the first battalion of the eighth regiment, the light battalion Stengel and the Kurprinz Chevauxlegers, barely 180 horses strong; the rest stood in reserve in and near Iglau under General Count Franz Minuzzi. Völderndorff calls the Bavarians 'the small band'. He gives no total for 5 December.
claims.rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images. The figures of 29 November precede the arrival of reinforcements that Völderndorff reports in the OCR (the 4th Chevauxlegers on the first day of December, a dragoon regiment from Mezanelli's brigade and the guns left at Mautern) and are not side A's strength on 5 December; he gives the number of horse Wrede drew up at the Sandhöfe in the OCR only, so it is not restated. The force was what Bernadotte's departure left Wrede, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'therefore even Davoust had to hasten up from Pressburg, Hungary being quiet, and Marshal Bernadotte with the divisions Kellermann, Drouet and Rivaud speedily (29th November) toward Brünn'; 'only the Bavarians were left facing Archduke Ferdinand's army corps'; 'General Wrede did have three regiments of cavalry with him, but among them barely 400 horses fit for service; besides, no more than 4,500 men of foot with six guns'; footnote, 'just as many guns he had had to leave behind at Mautern, on orders received, to cover the army's baggage'; 'for the arrival of Mezanelli's brigade could be possible only in five days, that of General Karg in seven; likewise the 4th Chevauxlegers Regiment Bubenhofen could arrive only after four days'; 'one battalion of the 7th Line Regiment held the market town itself, with outposts ahead of it, the other battalion the heights behind it'; 'to the left of the place stood the first and second battalions of the third Line Regiment (Herzog Karl), between them the light battalion Dietfurth, and in front the 2nd Regiment of Chevauxlegers with a battery'; 'to the right of the place were posted first the second, then at Wonnau the first battalion of the eighth regiment, between the two the light battalion Stengel, and in their support the regiment of Kurprinz Chevauxlegers'; 'the rest of the troops stood as reserve in and near Iglau under General Count Franz Minuzzi'; 'the Kurprinz Chevauxlegers Regiment (barely 180 horses strong)'; 'the small band of the Bavarians' (p. 299).

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), its own account in Schönhals: after the Archduke's junction with Hohenzollern's cavalry at Czaslau on the 24th (of November), reinforcements had raised his corps to 13 battalions and about 18 squadrons, 8294 men, of whom 1292 horse, by a report of the Archduke that Schönhals does not date; he refers to his appendices for the order of battle of 26 November (Beilage 35) and the state of the corps at the end of November (Beilage 37). For the attack of the 5th: a left column under Colonel Vacquant of 3 battalions and 2 squadrons, a centre under FML Hohenzollern of 4 battalions and 6 squadrons, and a reserve under General Dinersperg of 3 battalions and 4 squadrons; Deutschbrod was held by one battalion, and a side column that was not to attack covered the right flank. His footnote lists also a right column under Colonel Civallart (2 battalions, 3 squadrons of Rosenberg chevauxlegers, half a cavalry battery) and the side column under Colonel Plouquet (1 battalion, 2 squadrons of Blankenstein hussars), and gives the reserve's cavalry as cuirassier detachments.
claims.rationale: Side B's history, read from the page images. The footnote's five columns hold 13 battalions (our arithmetic), besides the battalion left at Deutschbrod; the text names only three columns, and the difference is not explained in the passages read. The appendices were not inspected. The Archduke formed the columns for his attack, so the claim is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): 'on the 20th the Archduke arrived at Wlaschim and on the 24th joined at Czaslau the Hohenzollern cavalry, which was 1098 horses strong'; 'the corps had grown through the reinforcements arriving one after another to 13 battalions and about 18 squadrons, whose strength according to a report of the Archduke was 8294 men, of whom 1292 horse'; 'appendix 35 gives the order of battle of the corps on 26 November'; 'appendix 37 gives the state of the corps at the end of November'; 'it was made in three columns: the first or left, under Colonel Vacquant, consisted of 3 battalions, 2 squadrons, the centre, which marched on the high road, under FML Hohenzollern, of 4 battalions, 6 squadrons'; 'General Dinersperg commanded the reserve; it was 3 battalions, 4 squadrons strong'; 'Deutschbrod remained occupied with one battalion; the right flank was covered by a side column, which was not to attack'; footnote, 'left column: Colonel Vacquant, 3 battalions Gemmingen, 2 squadrons Latour, ½ cavalry battery. Centre: FML Hohenzollern, GM Wratislaw, 1 battalion Reuss-Greiz, 1 battalion Reuss-Plauen, 1 battalion Erbach, 1 battalion Colloredo, 4 squadrons Hohenlohe dragoons, 2 squadrons Merveldt uhlans. Right column: Colonel Civallart, 1 battalion Maximilian, 1 battalion Gemmingen, 3 squadrons Rosenberg chevauxlegers, ½ cavalry battery. Reserve: General Dinersperg, 1 battalion Rainer, 2 battalions Stuart, cuirassier detachments of Mack, Hohenzollern, Albert. Side column: Colonel Plouquet, 1 battalion Froon, 2 squadrons Blankenstein hussars'.

claims.value: Wrede commanded side A. In Völderndorff, two days before, deprived of hope of support and outflanked, he had rejected a retreat and resolved to stay and attack, to break the enemy's centre and force him to draw back his wings, so delaying the Bavarians' destruction and gaining time, and on 3 December had attacked from Pfauendorf. For 5 December he had drawn Stecken, remote as it was, into his line of defence, partly to keep his opponent from coming too close to Iglau (OCR), partly to deny him the plain, since in the defiles he could resist with fewer men; he entrusted the defence of the position to Colonel Count Preysing, Major von Lindenau commanded the outpost line, and General Count Franz Minuzzi the reserve in and near Iglau. Seeing his left wing in full retreat and his centre and right in an unfavourable position, Wrede ordered all parts to fall back to defend Iglau before the enemy could get there first (OCR); while Minuzzi led the infantry to Iglau, Wrede took the head of all the cavalry to cover the retreat across the plain, drew it up at the Sandhöfe and made it swear to die rather than abandon the infantry and artillery to the enemy (OCR). The Bavarians held there from four in the afternoon until half past two the next morning, until the infantry with artillery and baggage had formed before Iglau and continued its retreat through the town toward Budwitz in good order.
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions as Völderndorff gives them, read from the page images except the start of the sentence on the line (p. 295), the retreat order, the cavalry and the oath (p. 298) and the preface (OCR). Völderndorff names among his sources the official reports of the commanders, above all the Bavarian ones, and the communications of Field Marshal Prince Wrede (preface, OCR), so for Wrede's decisions he may rest on Wrede's own account. Schönhals names Wrede only as the commander left behind and as the one who later told the Archduke of Austerlitz and denounced their truce (claims schoenhals-side-a and bodart-winner). The decision of 3 December led to a separate action, not this engagement. English renderings (ours): 'now, robbed of all prospect of near support, and already outflanked left and right by the enemy masses, there seemed no choice left but between a retrograde movement and the destruction of the Bavarian force'; 'Lieutenant-General Wrede rejected the thought of the former, which could have had the most ruinous influence on the undertakings of the great army, from which he had been without any news for five days'; 'he took the resolution to stay, to attack the enemy, to break through his centre, and in this way to force him to draw back his already advanced wings too'; 'thereby, if not prevented, the destruction was at least delayed and time gained'; 'the troops were (3rd December) drawn up at Pfauendorf, then led to the attack'; 'Wrede, partly so as not to allow his opponent too close an approach' (p. 295, OCR) 'to Iglau, partly so as not to concede him the advantage of the plain for the easier deployment of all his forces, had drawn Stecken, remote as it was, into his line of defence' (p. 296); 'here in the defiles he could resist more easily with fewer men'; 'he had entrusted the defence of this position to Colonel Count Preysing'; 'Major von Lindenau held the command of the whole chain of outposts'; as in claim voelderndorff-side-a for the reserve; 'but when Wrede now saw the left wing already in full retreat, the centre and the right wing in an unfavourable position against the superior enemy, he ordered the retrograde movement of all parts to the defence of Iglau, before the enemy could forestall him there' (OCR); 'while Minuzzi led all the infantry to Iglau, Lieutenant-General Wrede put himself at the head of all the cavalry, to cover the retreat, dangerous across the plain' (OCR); 'only at the edge of the wood lying between Stecken and Pfauendorf, in the fields by the so-called Sandhöfe, was he able [to form] this cavalry' (OCR); 'here he demanded of them the oath to perish rather than through cowardice to abandon the whole infantry and artillery to the enemy' (OCR); as in claim voelderndorff-side-b for the stand at the Sandhöfe; preface, 'the sources from which I drew above all the details of my picture were the various archives, the official reports of the various commanders, in particular the Bavarian commanders, and their written and oral accounts' (OCR); '[among them] His Highness Field Marshal Prince Wrede' (OCR).

claims.value: Archduke Ferdinand commanded side B and decided the attack. In Schönhals, on learning that the I French Corps had left, he resolved to use this weakening of the enemy for an attack; on 1 December he moved his headquarters to Deutschbrod; the general attack was decided for the 5th, in columns under Colonel Vacquant (left), FML Hohenzollern (centre) and General Dinersperg (reserve), all to be ready by noon; the left wing began the attack from Smilau by Bosowitz, Stöcken was attacked in its right flank and turned on its left by a detachment of Rosenberg chevauxlegers; the left wing and centre pressed on against the Wonau position while the right advanced by Wokolczan (OCR); at Pfauendorf the left wing turned the game park while it was attacked in front. In Völderndorff, the Archduke resolved to attack and destroy the Bavarians with all his forces and to march in the rear of the French (OCR); the brigade he had sent toward Windig-Jenikau could have taken Iglau in the Bavarians' rear and cut off their retreat, and the Bavarians owed it to luck alone that it did not, though this is said to have been the Archduke's order (OCR); he commanded the centre in person, Feldzeugmeister Count Kollowrath the left wing and General Count Hohenzollern the right.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as both accounts give them (page images except Völderndorff's resolution and brigade sentences and Schönhals's sentence on the Wonau position, OCR). The accounts differ on who led the wings: Völderndorff has Kollowrath lead the left and Hohenzollern the right, Schönhals has Vacquant lead the left column and Hohenzollern the centre. Schönhals's account of Austerlitz names an FML Count Kollowrat as the commander of an allied column on 2 December (OCR); the passages read do not say whether Völderndorff's Feldzeugmeister is the same man. English renderings (ours): Schönhals, 'no sooner did the Archduke learn of the departure of the 1st enemy corps than he resolved to use this weakening of the enemy for an attack'; 'on 1 December he moved his headquarters to Deutschbrod'; 'for the 5th the general attack on the enemy was decided'; as in claim schoenhals-side-b for the columns; 'the left column assembled at Smilau, the two others behind Blumendorf, the reserve on the height before Deutschbrod; all were to be ready at noon'; 'the left wing began the attack, for which it advanced from Smilau by Bosowitz'; 'this place was attacked in the right flank and turned on the left by a detachment of Rosenberg chevauxlegers; the enemy had to evacuate it with considerable loss'; 'after these advantages the left wing and the centre,' (p. 174) 'which followed the road, continued their attacking movements with much resolution against the position of Wonau, while the right advanced by ... (OCR) Wokolczan, so that the enemy was forced to leave his position with loss and in disorder' (p. 175) (OCR); 'at Pfauendorf, where ponds and a large game park narrow the ground very much and the pursuing column was confined to the high road, the enemy tried to make a stand once more; but the left wing went round the game park while at the same time its attack in front took place'; Völderndorff, 'Archduke Ferdinand, on the other hand, to whom the small number of the Bavarians, their abandonment, their distance from the main army and the non-arrival of Mezanelli's brigade were known, who knew the day of the decisive battle between the main armies to be near, resolved to undertake with all his forces the attack and destruction of the Bavarians and the march in the rear of the French power' (OCR); 'the Austrian brigade could therefore, at the moment when the Archduke attacked the Bavarians at Stecken, take Iglau in their rear and cut off the retreat' (OCR); 'that it did not happen, although it is said to have been the Archduke's order, the Bavarians had to thank the favour of fortune alone for' (OCR); 'Archduke Ferdinand commanded the centre in person, Feldzeugmeister Count' (p. 296) 'Kollowrath the left, General Count Hohenzollern the right wing' (p. 297); Schönhals on Austerlitz, 'FML Count Kollowrat' (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side B (Austrian) under Archduke Ferdinand over side A (Bavarian) under GM Wrede on 5 December. Schönhals: the Bavarians had to evacuate Stöcken with considerable loss and were forced to leave the Wonau position with loss and in disorder (OCR), were thrown out of the wood at Pfauendorf, and, favoured by darkness, retreated quickly and evacuated Iglau in the night; the Austrians occupied it at once, the Archduke moved his headquarters there on the 6th, and the Bavarian rearguard could be reached only at Budwitz. Völderndorff: the Bavarians held their position at the Sandhöfe from four in the afternoon until half past two the next morning, until their infantry with artillery and baggage had formed before Iglau and continued its retreat through the town toward Budwitz in the greatest order; their cavalry's third attack pushed the tired enemy back to his former position, and he no longer dared disturb the retreat (OCR). Schönhals adds that the Archduke won these advantages without knowing of Austerlitz, which had decided the campaign; after a truce of 48 hours, Bernadotte's threat to drive him from Iglau and Wrede's denunciation of the truce, he evacuated Iglau, and the prisoners taken at Stöcken were returned, having been taken while the armistice was already in force.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side B won), read from Bodart's entry, with the other accounts' ending (page images except the Wonau position and the cavalry's third attack, OCR). Both accounts have side A give up Stecken and Iglau and retreat toward Budwitz; Völderndorff stresses the ordered retreat its rearguard covered. The evacuation of Iglau under the armistice concerns the campaign, not the tactical result. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; '1805 5/12. action at Steken (6.)'; Schönhals, as in claim side-b-command for Stöcken and Wonau; 'the enemy was thrown out of the wood'; 'favoured by the darkness, the enemy continued his retreat quickly; he evacuated Iglau in the night, which the Austrians occupied at once, and the Archduke moved his headquarters there on the 6th'; 'the enemy, pursued on both the Brünn and the Vienna road, had so hurried his retreat that his rearguard could be reached only at Budwitz'; 'the Archduke won these advantages without knowledge of the great events that had decided the fate of the campaign at Austerlitz and brought about the truce'; 'still ignorant of the terms of the armistice, he himself concluded a truce of 48 hours, under which both sides were to remain in possession of the ground their troops held'; 'Hohenzollern met him at Austerlitz; but Bernadotte would hear of no other armistice terms than those concluded between the two emperors, and even threatened to attack the Archduke and drive him out of Iglau by force'; 'since at the same time Wrede denounced the truce, the Archduke saw himself compelled to yield to circumstances and evacuate Iglau'; 'the prisoners of war taken in the action at Stöcken were given back, since they had fallen into captivity while the armistice was already in force'; Völderndorff, as in claim voelderndorff-side-b for the Sandhöfe; 'for the tired enemy was pushed back into his former position, and he no longer dared to disturb further the retreat of the brave troops, who had achieved the incredible' (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart describes Steken as a market town in Bohemia, 10 km south of Deutsch-Brod. Völderndorff: Stecken lies in hilly country some distance from Iglau, with a broad plain from there to the town (OCR); Wrede drew it into his line to deny his opponent the plain, since in the defiles he could resist with fewer men; a thick wood hid the enemy's movements from the outposts; apart from the high road from Stecken to Iglau, every side road in this broken country was impassable for guns (OCR); the retreat ran through the wood between Stecken and Pfauendorf to the fields at the Sandhöfe and across the plain (OCR), and the cavalry fought by bright moonlight (OCR). Schönhals: side A's position at Wonau lay on both sides of the road, its wings resting on almost impenetrable woods; the wooded ground prevented a pursuit with cavalry; at Pfauendorf ponds and a large game park narrowed the ground and confined the pursuing column to the high road; darkness favoured side A's retreat.
claims.rationale: Ground, light and cover from Bodart's location and the two accounts (page images except the sentences marked OCR, whose distance from Iglau is not restated); no map was inspected. claims.value: Both accounts place side A in positions at Stecken (Stöcken) and Wonau, with a battalion in the market town and another on the heights behind (Völderndorff), on both sides of the road with its wings on almost impenetrable woods (Schönhals); neither names works from which side A fought.
claims.rationale: Code none_named: no passage read names works. The market town, the heights, the defiles and the woods are ground, not works; none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): as in claims voelderndorff-side-a, side-a-command and schoenhals-side-a.

open_questions: Deferred: Schönhals's appendices (Beilagen 35 and 37, the Archduke's order of battle of 26 November and his corps' state at the end of November) and the Archduke's report he cites, none inspected; Wrede's reports and his order of the day, which Völderndorff mentions, and the enemy admission he cites for the Austrian loss; French accounts, which the passages read do not cite; Völderndorff's narrative of the outpost fights of 28 November to 2 December and of the action of 3 December (OCR, cited only for Wrede's decision and the ammunition); his list of men mentioned for the action and his account of 6 December (read and not cited); Völderndorff's brief account of Hollabrunn and Dürnstein (read in the follow-up and not cited). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: Völderndorff's distance of Stecken from Iglau, the horse Wrede drew up at the Sandhöfe, Rechberg's horsemen, the hours of the evening fight, the date of the brigade sent to Windig-Jenikau and the losses of the outpost fights and of 3 December; Schönhals's dates and numbers for the outpost fights and Scheibler's raid; the page numbers of the OCR quotes.

Most consequential gap: side A's strength on 5 December. Bodart gives 10 battalions, 8 squadrons and 7,000 men; Völderndorff gives Wrede 4,500 foot, barely 400 serviceable horses and six guns on 29 November, before reinforcements he reports in the OCR, and lists the units posted on the 5th without a total; Schönhals gives no figure. The targeted follow-up searched Völderndorff's OCR from the middle of p. 250 to p. 283 for figures of men, horses, battalions, squadrons and guns and found none for Wrede's corps there. Side B's strength is also open: Bodart 11,000; Schönhals 13 battalions and about 18 squadrons, 8294 men, after the junction at Czaslau on 24 November; Völderndorff 17 battalions, 2,000 horse and 40 guns, and an enemy army of 30,000. Wrede's returns for early December or Schönhals's Beilage 37 could narrow them.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side B's strength (Bodart 11,000; Schönhals 8294; Völderndorff 30,000, with 17 battalions, 2,000 horse and 40 guns, which Bodart follows); side B's loss (Bodart 800; Völderndorff 756 by the enemy's admission; Schönhals 27 dead, 142 wounded and 36 missing, 205 by our arithmetic); side A's loss (Bodart about 1,000; Völderndorff 130 officers, 791 men and 56 horses killed, wounded and missing; Schönhals 20 officers and about 1000 men as prisoners besides many dead and wounded); the Austrian wing commanders (Völderndorff: the Archduke in the centre, Kollowrath left, Hohenzollern right; Schönhals: Vacquant left, Hohenzollern centre, Dinersperg reserve); the days before (Völderndorff: a Bavarian attack on Stecken on 3 December; Schönhals: outpost fights with small advantages on both sides until the 4th); Wrede's rank (GM in Bodart, Generallieutenant in Völderndorff); the manner of side A's retreat (Schönhals: in disorder and so hurried that its rearguard was reached only at Budwitz; Völderndorff: in the greatest order, covered by the cavalry until the next morning).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 17 battalions, 2,000 horse and 40 guns for side B are Völderndorff's, his losses agree with Völderndorff's rounded up, and his 11,000 and his figures for side A are not in the passages read); Völderndorff (the Bavarian history of 1826 by a major of the Bavarian general staff, written on higher orders from archives, the official reports of the commanders, above all the Bavarian ones, and the communications of Field Marshal Prince Wrede among others, by its preface; an interested account of side A); Schönhals (the Austrian account written in 1831 and printed in 1873, which cites the Archduke's report and its appendices for side B's strength). No passage read shows dependence between Völderndorff and Schönhals.
